stemBlocks.value: The diagram shows triangle ABC with A(-2, 5), B(-4, -3) and C(6, -1). M is the midpoint of AB and N is the midpoint of AC. (a) Determine the coordinates of M and N. (b) Calculate the lengths MN and BC. (c) Show that MN is parallel to BC. (d) State the relationship between the lengths MN and BC.
Think first: This is the midpoint theorem in coordinates — find M and N first and every later part follows from them.

solutionSteps.instruction: Find M, the midpoint of A(-2, 5) and B(-4, -3).
Find N, the midpoint of A(-2, 5) and C(6, -1).
Compare the gradients of MN and BC.

contentBlocks.value: Result: Equal gradients, so MN is parallel to BC

strategyBlocks.value: Average coordinates to get M and N, use the distance formula for MN and BC, compare gradients to prove the lines are parallel, then compare the two lengths.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) M(-3, 1) and N(2, 2)  (b) MN = √26 ≈ 5.10 units, BC = √104 = 2√26 ≈ 10.20 units  (c) Both gradients equal 1/5, so MN is parallel to BC  (d) MN is half the length of BC.

whyThisWorks.value: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is always parallel to the third side and exactly half its length — the midpoint theorem. In coordinates, halving both the horizontal and the vertical step scales the whole segment by ½ without changing its direction, which is why the gradients come out identical and the lengths come out in the ratio 1 : 2. Equal gradients are the proof of parallelism; the diagram alone is not.

commonErrors.misconception: Proving parallelism by saying the lines “look parallel” instead of showing equal gradients.
